domain_description: Pedagogical traditions that don't all originate in — or get evaluated by — Western meta-analytic research: Singapore Math's Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract sequence, Marton's Variation Theory (developed in Sweden and Hong Kong), Finnish phenomenon-based learning, Reggio Emilia's documentation practice, Ubuntu collective-knowledge tasks, Indigenous place-based inquiry, and the culturally responsive teaching tradition built on Banks, Gay, Ladson-Billings and Hammond. Editorial note: Western meta-analytic standards apply unevenly to non-Western pedagogical traditions. Variation Theory and CPA carry robust meta-analyses; culturally responsive teaching has a growing meta-analytic base; Ubuntu, Reggio, and place-based pedagogies operate in interpretive scholarly traditions without standardised effect sizes. We show that gap honestly rather than excluding traditions for not being measured on Western terms — the gap is partly a measurement problem, not always a quality problem.

skills.description: Design tasks built on Marton's Variation Theory — make critical features of a concept discernible by holding everything constant except the feature you want students to see. Four patterns: contrast (varying values to reveal an aspect), separation (varying one aspect while others are fixed), generalization (varying surface appearance while the principle is fixed), fusion (varying multiple critical aspects simultaneously). Anchored on the meta-analysis of the underlying mechanism — comparing cases and contrasting examples — at d=0.50 (Alfieri et al. 2013). The pedagogical theory (Marton, Pang, Kullberg, Runesson) has a substantial Hong Kong and Swedish learning-study tradition built around it, but that tradition reports outcomes in interpretive case-study form rather than pooled effect sizes — so we anchor on the mechanism meta-analysis.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Variation theory task design requires the teacher to identify the critical features of a concept (often non-obvious) and design tasks where those features are systematically varied while irrelevant ones are held constant. The discipline is taught most effectively through Learning Study cycles — small teams of teachers planning, teaching, and analysing the same lesson in iteration. Roughly 8–15 hours of structured PD per cycle, but the design discipline transfers across subjects and year groups once internalised. NCETM's UK Teaching for Mastery uses variation as one of its five "Big Ideas" — schools already inside that programme have most of the infrastructure. Source-age caveat: Alfieri et al. 2013 is the cleanest meta-analytic anchor for the mechanism (comparing cases / contrasting examples, d=0.50) but is 13 years old. Searches in the 5-year and 10-year windows found no newer quality meta-analysis on the same construct; the variation-theory literature 2017+ (Kullberg, Marton, Pang, Runesson) is rich but operates in interpretive learning-study tradition without pooled effect sizes.

skills.description: Design a Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract learning sequence — start with manipulatives that let students physically model the concept (Cuisenaire rods, base-10 blocks, fraction bars), move to pictorial representations that preserve the structural relationships (bar models, number lines, area diagrams), then connect to abstract symbolic notation. Built on Bruner's enactive-iconic-symbolic theory and operationalised in Singapore Maths via the bar-model method. Anchored on Sokolowski (2018) meta-analysis of representations in elementary mathematics at g=0.53. Two caveats: a more recent meta on multiple-vs-single representations across all mathematical domains (Liu, Ji & Guo 2026, Educational Psychology Review) found a more modest g=0.29; and the EEF's RCT of UK Mathematics Mastery (which used CPA-based Inspire Maths) showed smaller programme-level effects than the Singapore literature suggests. Effects depend heavily on whether the abstract phase actually arrives — manipulatives held too long, or not connected back to symbolic notation, lose the effect.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Manipulatives have a one-off material cost (Cuisenaire rods, base-10 blocks, fraction bars — roughly 200–500 SEK per classroom set, or free with paper-based alternatives). The real cost is teacher PD: knowing which manipulative maps to which concept, when to fade from concrete to pictorial, and how to verbalise the connection to abstract notation. Singapore Math programmes (Inspire Maths, Maths — No Problem!, Math in Focus) bundle materials with structured PD; commitment is typically a 2–3 year curriculum adoption with ongoing teacher training. Carbonneau, Marley & Selig 2013's key moderator: studies with high instructional guidance produced larger effects than low-guidance studies — manipulatives in students' hands without explicit teacher framing do not produce the effect. Source-recency note: Sokolowski 2018 is the cleanest construct match (elementary math representations) and falls within the 10-year window; the more recent Liu, Ji & Guo 2026 found a smaller g=0.29 across a broader scope (multi vs single representations in all maths domains).

skills.description: Redesign a lesson to centre students' cultural backgrounds, community knowledge, and lived experience in the curriculum, in instruction, and in classroom interaction. Built on Gay's culturally responsive teaching, Ladson-Billings' culturally relevant pedagogy, Paris & Alim's culturally sustaining pedagogy, and Hammond's "ready for rigor" framework. Honest evidence note: the most-cited review — Aronson & Laughter (2016) Review of Educational Research — is a qualitative synthesis of 45 empirical studies that consistently found positive student outcomes across content areas; it is not a pooled meta-analysis and reports no Cohen's d. The most recent quantitative meta-analysis (Cipriano et al. 2024 culturally responsive SEL) covered only 7 studies on SEL outcomes, not academic achievement primarily. The construct has 30+ years of conceptual scholarship and converging qualitative evidence; what it does not yet have is a robust Western-style pooled effect size on academic outcomes. We include the card with that gap visible because excluding it would treat measurement as a synonym for quality.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Implementing CRT is not a checklist of activities — it requires sustained professional learning on (1) cultural self-awareness, (2) knowledge of students' communities and out-of-school knowledge bases, (3) curricular redesign that integrates cultural content authentically rather than as add-on tokenism, and (4) classroom interaction patterns (questioning, discussion norms, error response) that support cultural identity. Hammond's Culturally Responsive Teaching and the Brain framework estimates 2–3 years of consistent PD for the practice to become embedded, with leadership-level commitment to curriculum review. Quick-fix CRT (multicultural celebration days, surface "diverse" examples) reliably fails to produce outcome effects — that is part of why the quantitative evidence base remains thin: the construct is operationalised so differently across studies that pooled effect sizes have not been credibly computed.

skills.description: Anchor curriculum learning in a specific local place — built environment, ecosystem, community, heritage — so students develop subject knowledge through the place rather than abstracted from it. Two traditions converge here: Sobel and Gruenewald's community-and-ecology-focused place-based education, which has a substantial meta-analytic base (Van de Wetering et al. 2022 found g=0.38 on attitudes and g=0.41 on behavior across 169 studies and 176,007 participants in 43 countries), and Castagno & Brayboy's Indigenous education tradition, which operates in interpretive scholarship without pooled effect sizes. The Indigenous tradition is not absent of evidence — it is evidenced differently. Use this skill when connecting academic content to students' local environment and heritage; pair with culturally responsive teaching when working with Indigenous, immigrant, or heritage-rich communities.
skills.effect_d_source: van de Wetering, Leijten, Spitzer & Thomaes
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Doesn't require special materials — the place is the material — but does require teacher time to (1) map curriculum standards to local-place opportunities, (2) build relationships with community partners (farms, museums, elders, municipal departments), and (3) handle logistics of out-of-classroom learning when relevant. Initial mapping is roughly 10–20 hours per teacher per subject; afterwards the place-curriculum connections compound and reuse across cohorts. Indigenous place-based education requires additional time and the participation of community knowledge-holders — not something a teacher implements alone. Source-outcome note: Van de Wetering et al. 2022 reports four outcome-family effect sizes (knowledge g=0.95, attitudes g=0.38, intentions g=0.26, behavior g=0.41); the toolkit anchors on the attitudes outcome (g=0.38) because it is the closest analog to engagement and affect with content, avoids inflating from curriculum-test alignment (the knowledge outcome), and sits in the middle of the meta's reported spread.

skills.description: Audit an educational practice for cultural assumptions and cross-cultural validity. Ask the WEIRD questions (Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan 2010): does the evidence base for this practice rest on Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic samples? What does it assume about parent-school relationships, classroom hierarchy, individual-versus-collective achievement, learning-as-display-of-knowledge? Where does it not transfer? Use when adapting curricula for diverse contexts, when questioning a "universal" practice claim, or when reviewing whether US/UK research generalises to a Swedish (or any non-WEIRD-default) context. Framework, not intervention — no Cohen's d applies; the value is in better adoption decisions and avoiding the install of practices whose evidence base doesn't generalise. The bias has persisted (Nielsen et al. 2017 found roughly 90% of developmental-psych samples still WEIRD a decade after the original paper); the Deffner, Rohrer & McElreath 2022 causal-modelling framework provides tools for thinking through which findings should and shouldn't generalise.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Doesn't require materials, PD investment, or curriculum change — it's a thinking discipline applied before adoption decisions. The cost is intellectual: leadership needs to be willing to look at evidence behind a "proven practice" and ask whether the proof transfers. Most useful at school and district decision points (curriculum adoption, programme rollout, technology procurement) where the savings from rejecting a poorly-transferring practice are large. Note on verification status: this is a framework, not an intervention, so the unverified tag is structural rather than a quality judgement — same pattern as TPACK Developer in the AI Learning Science domain. Not having a Cohen's d here is itself the point: practices that come with strong d-values from WEIRD samples may still fail in non-WEIRD contexts, so the framework warns specifically against treating high effect sizes as automatic warrants.

skills.description: Anchor a multidisciplinary teaching unit in a real-world phenomenon that requires multiple subject lenses to understand fully — climate, migration, food systems, urban planning, a particular building, a local river — so students engage subject content through the phenomenon rather than abstracted from it. The Finnish 2016 core curriculum (POPS-2016) makes at least one such multidisciplinary module per school year mandatory; the approach is associated with Lonka and the Helsinki research group. Honest evidence positioning: phenomenon-based learning as a broad pedagogy has no clean independent meta-analysis (Adipat 2024 is a conceptual review; Kreijkes & Greatorex 2024 found the integrated-curriculum review literature is methodologically weak). The closest meta-analytic proxy is its most-studied subset: STEM integration. Zhou, Dong & Wang's 2025 meta-analysis in Research in Science Education found integrated STEM produced a substantial achievement gain (g=0.66 across 40 studies, 15,577 students), with the largest effects from context integration (anchoring in a real phenomenon) and inquiry-based pedagogy — both core to phenomenon-based learning.
skills.implementation_cost_rationale: Requires whole-school commitment, not single-teacher adoption: coordinated multidisciplinary modules need timetable changes, joint planning time across subject teachers, leadership willingness to accept that not every subject hour produces a discrete subject lesson, and assessment frameworks that recognise cross-disciplinary competence (often poorly served by national subject-by-subject tests). The Finnish implementation took 5+ years of sustained PD and curriculum redesign at school level; smaller-scale pilot adoption is possible but typically delivers smaller effects. Zhou et al. 2025's moderator finding is the lever to focus on: anchor in a real-world context (phenomenon-based, the strong mover) rather than just content coordination across subjects, and use inquiry-based pedagogy over project-based. Source-construct caveat: the toolkit anchors on STEM integration as proxy because phenomenon-based learning broadly has no clean meta-analysis — Adipat 2024 is a conceptual review and the broader integrated-curriculum review literature was assessed as methodologically weak by Kreijkes & Greatorex 2024. The STEM-integration meta captures the cross-disciplinary mechanism but not the humanities/arts side of full Finnish PBL.
